analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to affirmatively approve major federal regulations before they can take effect.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee advanced the bill to the floor calendar in October 2017, but it never received a vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal agencies issue the rules that carry out laws on clean air and water, workplace safety, banking, food, and drugs. Under this bill, any rule the government labels "major" — generally one affecting the economy by $100 million or more, or significantly raising costs or prices — could not take effect unless both the House and Senate passed a separate law approving it within 70 working days, and the President signed it. The approval bills could not be amended, and any rule that did not get approved in time simply never took effect. In practice, most major rules would die not by being voted down but because Congress failed to act.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that would otherwise face costly federal rules — polluters, financial firms, large employers — benefit, because a rule only binds them if Congress affirmatively passes a law approving it within a 70-day window, something that would rarely happen. It also gives members of Congress a recorded vote they can take against any unpopular regulation.

how_it_helps.text: Every major federal rule would require a joint resolution of approval, enacted into law within 70 session or legislative days, before it could take effect; an unapproved rule "shall not take effect."
Approval resolutions would be fast-tracked, barred from amendment, and must be voted on by fixed deadlines, giving opponents and supporters a direct up-or-down vote.
Agencies would have to publish the information behind each rule — data, studies, cost-benefit analyses, and estimated jobs added or lost — before the rule could take effect.
The bill exempts monetary policy and lets the President let a major rule take effect for 90 days in emergencies, including imminent threats to health or safety.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal regulation would bear the cost: clean air and water rules, workplace safety standards, consumer financial protections, and food and drug safety rules large enough to be "major" could each be killed by congressional inaction, even without a vote against them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on federal protections

drawbacks.text: The bill flips regulation from default-on to default-off: any major rule Congress fails to approve within the 70-day clock "shall not take effect" [S3], so a rule needed to protect the public can die through inaction alone, with no recorded vote and no chance to fix it.

Approval resolutions cannot be amended at any stage [S3], so Congress could not improve a flawed rule — it could only approve or kill it as written, and unrelated political fights would determine whether each rule survived.

The standard is broad: a rule counts as "major" if it has an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, raises costs or prices significantly, or affects competition, employment, investment, or productivity [S2][S3], which sweeps in most significant health, safety, environmental, and consumer protections.

Even supporters would acknowledge the cost of regulatory uncertainty: businesses and agencies would face a layer of political timing on top of the rulemaking process, and rules could be approved or killed based on the politics of the moment rather than their merits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated rationale — that Congress has delegated too much lawmaking to unelected agencies and should vote on the biggest rules — is a real accountability argument. But the design answers that argument in the bluntest way possible: instead of making Congress legislate better, it makes major regulation fail by default. A rule protecting air, water, workers, or consumers would need two chambers and the President to agree, unamended, within 70 days — a bar most would never clear, regardless of merit. The practical effect would fall hardest on the public protections the rules deliver, while the industries those rules restrain would gain the most.

outcome.mechanism: The Homeland Security committee reported the bill favorably in October 2017 and it was placed on the Senate's floor calendar, but no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill on January 4, 2017 with 39 Republican cosponsors.

The bill defines a "major rule" as one with an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more, a major increase in costs or prices, or significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, or innovation.

Under the bill, a major rule takes effect only if Congress enacts a joint resolution of approval within 70 session or legislative days; otherwise the rule is deemed not approved and does not take effect.

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee ordered the bill reported favorably in May 2017 and formally reported it, with amendments and minority views filed by committee Democrats, on October 16, 2017.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 239) on October 16, 2017, and no further action was taken before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never reached a vote, the default system survived: federal agencies kept their authority to issue major health, safety, environmental, and consumer rules, and the industries that would have gained a veto over those rules got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public they protect

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee's Democratic members filed minority views against the bill; the Senate never voted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Polluting industries (coal, oil and gas, chemical manufacturers)
industries.note: Major environmental rules — limits on air and water pollution or toxic emissions — would need an affirmative act of Congress within 70 days to take effect, which would rarely happen. The industry's gain comes directly at the cost of the public protections the rules deliver.

Major consumer-protection and financial rules would be subject to the same approval requirement, letting Congress let them die by inaction. The industry's interest runs against the consumers those rules protect.

industries.industry: Large employers facing workplace-safety and wage rules
industries.note: Safety and labor rules large enough to be "major" could be blocked without a recorded vote. Workers would bear the cost of whatever rules did not survive.

Agencies would lose their core power to put major rules into effect on their own, making them dependent on Congress for each significant rule. Their interest here runs alongside the public's, since the rules they write are the protections ordinary people rely on.
